Strategic Response of News Publishers to Generative AI

Hangcheng Zhao (Rutgers) · Ron Berman (Wharton)

Working Paper, 2026

Three responses examined: crawler access policies · content format choices · hiring patterns

Hook: ~75% of top news publishers slammed the door on GenAI crawlers via robots.txt. The intuition: stop them scraping our content. This paper asks — did it work?

Why this room: a clean strategic-response setting — a new technology shock, an observable defensive action, and a causal design to price it.

Roadmap: the headline is counterintuitive — blocking is followed by LOWER traffic. Then: content gets richer (not longer), and newsroom hiring holds.

Outline

  1. Crawler access policiesDoes disallowing GenAI bots in robots.txt protect traffic, or cut it? A priori the sign is unclear.
  2. Content format choicesDo publishers produce more text to compete, or shift to rich media that LLMs cannot replicate?
  3. Hiring patternsDoes editorial headcount contract as AI lowers the cost of producing content?

Pacing: most of the time goes to analysis 1 (the blocking result + identification); that is the contribution. Content and hiring move fast.

Setting: data & sample

The shock window

  • Nov 2022 — ChatGPT launches.
  • May 2024 — Google AI Overviews.
  • Main causal analysis: pre-May 2024 (blocking concentrated mid-2023; cleanest ID).

Sample

  • 30 newspaper publishers (NAICS 513110) — ≈70% of top-500 Comscore news traffic.
  • Widened to the top-500 news publishers as a sample-robustness check on the traffic panels (Semrush, Comscore).

Real reason for this design: three independent traffic panels is the whole credibility play — bot-filtered (SimilarWeb/Semrush) plus a human-only panel (Comscore). If all three move together, the effect isn't just "we removed bot visits."

Push back on: 30 publishers is small; standard errors and the imprecise Comscore estimate flow from that.

Motivation: traffic is sliding

Daily total visits (SimilarWeb) & weekly visits by channel (Semrush), 30 publishers

What the data show

  • PELT change-point detection: a downward level shift after early 2023 (Fig 2).
  • Pre-May-2024 the decline is in direct visits; organic search holds (Fig 3a).
  • After May 2024 (AI Overviews) both channels fall (Fig 3b).

Fig 2: change-point detection, daily total traffic

Fig 3: weekly visits by channel (a/b)

Read aloud: the level shifts down after early 2023 — modest, but it coincides with the first wave of industry panic about LLM substitution.

Point at: the step-down in the series; that early break motivates "publishers will respond."

Pushback: is early-2023 really GenAI, or post-COVID news-traffic normalization? The direct-vs-organic split is their answer.

Analysis 1: crawler access policies

Description

  • Adoption starts mid-2023, staggered thereafter.
  • OpenAI bots blocked first, then Anthropic, Perplexity.
  • ≈75% of sample blocks an OpenAI crawler at some point.

Analysis

  • News blocks far more than retail (<10% of top retailers).
  • Staggered timing → the engine for the DiD design.

News publishers: crawler-block adoption (staggered)

Top-100 retailers: blocking stays <10% (WA.1d)

Read aloud: three-quarters of these publishers blocked at least one GenAI crawler — this is a real, widespread strategic action, not a fringe choice.

Point at: the staircase shape — different publishers block at different weeks. That variation is what identifies the effect.

Pushback: robots.txt is voluntary (RFC 9309 — "not access authorization"); compliance is imperfect. So this is the effect of declaring a block, not of perfectly enforced exclusion.

Identification: staggered DiD

Challenge

Blockers and non-blockers differ, and all publishers face common time shocks. Naive before/after conflates blocking with the secular traffic slide.

Strategy

Callaway & Sant'Anna (2021): cohort = first week a publisher disallows any GenAI crawler. Compare each cohort to not-yet-treated + never-treated publishers.

$$\mathrm{ATT}(g,t)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[Y_{i,t}-Y_{i,g-1}\mid G_i=g\right]-\mathbb{E}\!\left[Y_{i,t}-Y_{i,g-1}\mid G_i>t\right]$$
  • $Y_{i,t}$: log weekly visits to publisher $i$ in week $t$
  • $G_i$: first blocking week (cohort); $G_i=\infty$ for never-blockers
  • Assumes: parallel trends, no anticipation, and no reversal (treatment absorbing). Two threats →

Plain English: absent blocking, a publisher's traffic would have moved like that of peers who hadn't yet blocked. The "not-yet-treated as controls" trick is what makes staggered timing usable.

Most plausible violation: publishers block because they see traffic sliding — reverse causality. They test this directly (next-slide robustness): lagged traffic growth does not predict adoption.

★ ~7% fewer weekly visits within 6 weeks of blocking — same magnitude across all three independent panels, including human-only browsing.

Read aloud: roughly a 7% drop, and crucially it shows up in Comscore's human panel too — so it isn't just the mechanical removal of bot hits.

Point at: flat pre-period coefficients, then a downward step after week 0 in all three panels.

Pushback: Comscore CI crosses zero (small panel). The claim rests on the consistency of the point estimates, not Comscore alone. Effect also fades after ~20 weeks.

Mechanism: why blocking hurts

Publisher blocks LLM
▼ ?
LLM mentions publisher less
▼
Consumers recall brand less
▼ ?
Direct visits decrease
Likely primary channel
No citations / links in answers
▼
LLM referrals decrease
Possible secondary channel
Evidence for the primary channel: pre-May-2024, the decline is concentrated in direct visits while organic-search referrals stay stable — consistent with lost brand exposure, not lost referral clicks.

The argument: blocking removes you from the answer box, so people who'd have seen your name don't think to type your URL — a brand-exposure loss that surfaces as fewer direct visits.

Honest read: this is an interpretation supported by the direct-vs-organic split, not a separately identified mechanism. The secondary referral channel is argued to be small for this period.

Two links carry a "?": (1) block → fewer LLM mentions is assumed, not audited — no study checks whether LLMs actually drop a blocked publisher; (2) weaker recall → fewer direct visits is shaky, since a reader who recalls the brand may still arrive through a habitual search route rather than typing the URL.

Log weekly visits; * p<0.1. Negative & significant only for the largest / highest-traffic tiers.

My doubt: the small tiers are mostly zeros

  • The null / wrong-signed estimates appear exactly where visits are lowest (≤1/day; ranks 101–500).
  • DV is log(visits), and those tiers have the most zero-visit weeks, which log drops or distorts.
  • So “blocking doesn’t hurt small publishers” may be an estimation artifact, not economics.
Ask the authors: re-estimate in levels (PPML); report the zero-visit share by tier. Why zeros are unreliable →

Read the table: the negative effect is significant only for Top-50 (Panel A) and higher-traffic (Panel B) publishers; it is null or wrong-signed for the smallest tiers.

The tell: the effect vanishes precisely in the tiers where zeros are densest (≤1 visit/day, ranks 101–500) — the same place log-OLS breaks down. Detail in the zeros appendix.

Robustness: is it really blocking?

1. No reverse causality

Discrete-time adoption regression: lagged traffic growth does not predict blocking (coef ≈ 0). Publishers don't block because they just lost traffic.

2. Placebo timing (×3 designs)

Re-randomized timing, control-only, and expanded-pool placebos all center at zero; the observed −7% sits in the left tail. Not an artifact of staggered timing.

3. No confounding robots.txt edits

19 of 24 blockers changed only GenAI directives; none touched Googlebot/Bingbot or paywalls. Flat pre-trends out to 24 weeks.

Why this matters: the whole result hinges on blocking not being a proxy for "a publisher in trouble." The adoption regression is the cleanest rebuttal to that story; the placebos rule out mechanical timing artifacts.

Every HTML tag is a measurable page element. GenAI-era pages add interactive, media & ad tags but fewer <article> units — richer format, less text.

Read aloud: no "AI slop" text flood — the opposite. Article and section tags fall ~31%, while interactive and ad-tech elements jump 50–68% relative to retailers.

Pushback: is heavier pages a GenAI differentiation strategy, or just the web getting heavier everywhere? The top-100-retail benchmark is doing the work — interactive grows faster than retail; multimedia and DOM do not.

Analysis 3: hiring patterns

Editorial vs other job postings, Revelio; gray line = ChatGPT (Nov 2022)

Editorial (solid) vs other (dashed) counts

Editorial share of postings

★ No post-GenAI drop in editorial postings (TWFE ATT = +7.58***). But the raw series is noisy; arguably "no clear difference from other roles," not affirmative evidence that hiring held.

Read aloud: if AI were replacing newsroom labor, editorial's share of postings should fall after ChatGPT. It doesn't — it ticks up.

Caveat: postings measure labor demand, not realized employment, and the window is short. "No short-run substitution," not "no substitution ever."

Interpretation to push on: the editorial series is messy; the "no decline" claim may really be an underpowered null (no detectable difference from the comparison roles), not positive evidence of stability. Watch the confidence bands, not just the point estimate.

Takeaways & Discussion

Takeaways

  • Blocking backfires: the most popular defense (robots.txt) is followed by ~7% fewer visits.
  • Differentiate, don't out-produce: rich/interactive media rises, text volume falls. No "slop."
  • No newsroom contraction yet. Editorial hiring share holds or rises.

Discussion questions

  1. Why do direct visits fall while organic search holds? Brand-recall loss, a measurement artifact (dark traffic read as direct), or selection on who blocks?
  2. What would make it truly causal? Two threats to the staggered DiD: (1) self-selection — blocking is chosen, not assigned; (2) reversal — status flips 1→0 when a publisher un-blocks, which the design assumes away. ← Identification
  3. Do LLM firms even honor the block? Training bots mostly comply; answer engines (Perplexity, Bytespider) evade, so the effect is compliance-weighted. See appendix →

30-second elevator: news publishers' favorite GenAI defense — blocking crawlers — is associated with losing ~7% of traffic; the response that seems to help is differentiating content, not blocking or flooding text.

Bridge to discussion: open on Q1 — is this the causal cost of blocking, or selection on who blocks when? Everything downstream rests on that.

Q1 options: recall-but-reroute (a recalled brand should still return via habitual search, not direct); dark traffic / app opens / bots misclassified as direct; reverse causality (blockers already shedding loyal audiences).

Q2 designs: vendor-default IV (default block template shifts blocking, not traffic directly); a named bot’s launch date as a natural experiment; within-publisher gap between robots-obeying and robots-ignoring bots.

Q3: see the compliance appendix — big training crawlers comply, but Perplexity/Bytespider evade and a block is prospective (cannot un-ingest trained/cached data).

Appendix: robots.txt compliance

Does a Disallow actually stop the crawler? Evidence on AI-bot compliance

Compliance with a full block

CrawlerTypeHonors block
GPTBottraining~100%
ClaudeBottraining~100%
Amazonbottraining~100%
ChatGPT-Useranswer~100%*
PerplexityBotanswer~20%
Applebotsearch~4%
Bytespiderscraper~3%

Duke, ACM IMC 2025 (arXiv:2505.21733), full Disallow: /. *ChatGPT-User disputed — TollBit finds ~42% non-compliant.

So does the block “work”?

  • Training bots comply with a full block; answer engines & scrapers evade (Perplexity stealth crawler, Cloudflare 2025). Even compliant bots ignore narrow rules (GPTBot ~30%).
  • A block is also prospective (cannot un-ingest cached data), so read the effect as compliance-weighted (ITT), not on/off.
Ties to the mechanism: the “block → fewer LLM mentions” arrow only holds where crawlers actually comply. ← back to mechanism

Why this appendix exists: the whole causal story assumes a block reduces the publisher’s presence in LLM outputs. That only holds if the crawler obeys the block.

Sharpest fact: Cloudflare ran a controlled test on fresh domains with a restrictive robots.txt and caught Perplexity evading via a Chrome-impersonating agent and rotating undeclared IPs.

Nuance: compliance is the norm for the big training bots; the failure mode is answer engines doing live retrieval at query time, plus already-ingested data.

Sources: Duke / ACM IMC 2025 (arXiv:2505.21733, per-bot compliance rates); Longpre et al. 2024 (NeurIPS, arXiv:2407.14933); Reuters Institute 2024; Bouchaud & Ramaciotti 2025 (arXiv:2510.09031); Wired 2024; Cloudflare 2025; TollBit 2025; RFC 9309.

Appendix: why log-with-zeros misleads

Why the smallest-tier null may be an artifact, not economics

The problem

  • log(0) is undefined. With many zero-visit weeks you must drop them or use log(1+x) / asinh.
  • The %-effect then depends on the transform and units chosen — not a well-defined causal parameter (Chen & Roth 2023).
  • Dropping zeros silently conditions on the extensive margin: a selected, intensive-only sample.

Why it bites the small tier — and the fix

  • ≤1 visit/day = the most zeros, where log-OLS is least reliable and low counts are noisiest to measure.
  • Fix: PPML / Poisson on levels uses the zeros with no transform (Santos Silva & Tenreyro 2006); report the zero-visit share by tier.
Read: PPML null → real heterogeneity; PPML negative → zeros artifact. ← back to Table 4

Sources: Chen & Roth 2023 (QJE); Santos Silva & Tenreyro 2006 (REStat, PPML); Cohn, Liu & Wardlaw 2022 (JFE); Mullahy & Norton 2024 (OBES); Bellemare & Wichman 2020 (OBES).

One-liner: the size gradient may be genuine or an artifact of running log(visits) where zeros cluster in the small tiers; PPML on levels plus zero-share by tier settles it.
